lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Lists of values: creating them, reading by position, adding and removing, and measuring with #.

sections.heading: One table, many values
sections.body:
A **table** is Luau's only way of grouping values, and it's used for everything: lists, records, modules, objects. The simplest use is an **array**, an ordered list. You write one with curly brackets and commas between the values.

Each value sits at a numbered position called an **index**. Luau counts from **1**, not 0 like many other languages, so the first item is at index 1. You read an item by putting its index in square brackets after the table's name.

example.caption: A list of streets
example.code:
local streets = { "Elm Road", "Mill Lane", "Crow Street" }
print(streets[1])
print(streets[3])
print(#streets)
example.explain: Prints `Elm Road`, `Crow Street`, then `3`, the number of items.

sections.heading: Changing an array
sections.body:
Assign to an index to replace the item there. To add to the end, use `table.insert(list, value)`. It can also insert at a position, `table.insert(list, 1, value)`, which shifts everything after it up by one.

`table.remove(list)` removes and returns the last item, and `table.remove(list, i)` removes the item at position i, shifting the later items down to close the gap. That shifting keeps the array tidy, with no empty slots in the middle.

example.caption: A queue of orders
example.code:
local queue = { "Hill", "Vance" }
table.insert(queue, "Okafor")
local nextUp = table.remove(queue, 1)
print(nextUp, #queue, queue[1])
example.explain: Prints `Hill 2 Vance`: Hill leaves the front, and everyone moves up.

sections.heading: Length with #
sections.body:
`#list` gives the number of items in an array. It's how you loop over every item with a numeric for loop from 1 to `#list`, and how you find the last item, at `list[#list]`.

`#` is only reliable for arrays without **holes**. A table can't store `nil`: assigning `nil` to an index removes that entry. If you set an item in the middle to `nil`, the array now has a gap, and `#` may report either side of it. So never "delete" from the middle of an array by assigning `nil`. Use `table.remove`, which closes the gap.

sections.heading: Reading past the end
sections.body:
Reading an index that has nothing in it isn't an error. It gives `nil`, the same as reading any missing value. So `streets[10]` on a three-item list is simply `nil`.

That's convenient, but it means a typo in an index or an off-by-one loop doesn't fail loudly. It quietly produces `nil`, which usually errors a few lines later in a more confusing place. When something is unexpectedly `nil`, check your indexes and loop limits first.

key_points: Arrays are tables with values at indexes 1, 2, 3 and so on.
`table.insert` adds and `table.remove` removes, shifting items to keep the list tidy.
`#list` counts the items, but only reliably when there are no holes.
Reading a missing index gives `nil`, not an error.
mistakes: Starting at index 0, which in Luau is just an ordinary key outside the array.
Setting a middle item to `nil` instead of using `table.remove`.
Looping to `#list + 1` or starting at 0, and processing a `nil`.
lessons.try_it: Make a list of five customer names. Print the first and last using `#`, add a sixth with `table.insert`, remove the second with `table.remove`, and print the list's length after each change.

quiz.question: What does `table.remove(t, 1)` do to `{ "a", "b", "c" }`?
choices: Removes `"a"` and moves the others down
quiz.explain: table.remove closes the gap, so b becomes item 1 and c item 2.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't you set a middle item of an array to `nil`?
choices: It creates a hole that makes `#` unreliable
quiz.explain: With a gap in the middle, the length operator may give either side of it.

lessons.title: Looping and the table library
lessons.summary: Going through every item, and the built-in functions for finding, sorting and joining.

sections.heading: Looping over an array
sections.body:
You can loop with a numeric for from 1 to `#list`. Luau also lets you loop over a table directly: `for index, value in list do`. On each run, `index` is the position and `value` is the item there, and for arrays it goes in order from 1. This is called **generalised iteration**.

You'll also see `for index, value in ipairs(list) do` in other code. `ipairs` goes through an array in order and stops at the first `nil`. Both work for arrays. Use an underscore as the name for anything you don't need, like the index when you only care about the values.

example.caption: Every item, with its position
example.code:
local stops = { "Bakery", "Clinic", "Old Mill" }
for index, stop in stops do
	print(index, stop)
end

sections.heading: Finding things
sections.body:
`table.find(list, value)` searches an array and returns the index of the first matching item, or `nil` if it isn't there. Since `nil` is falsy, it doubles as a yes-or-no check: `if table.find(blocked, name) then` means "if this name is in the blocked list".

It compares with `==`, so it finds exact values. To find the first item matching a rule, like the first order over 5 pizzas, write the loop yourself and `break`.

sections.heading: Sorting
sections.body:
`table.sort(list)` puts an array in order, smallest first, **in place**: it changes the list itself rather than returning a new one. Numbers sort numerically and strings alphabetically.

For any other order, pass a **comparison function** as the second argument. It receives two items and returns `true` if the first should come **before** the second. Sorting biggest first means returning whether a is greater than b. The function must use a strict comparison like `>`, never `>=`, or Luau can error with "invalid order function for sorting".

example.caption: Biggest tips first
example.explain: Prints `12 7 3`. The function says a comes first when it's bigger.

sections.heading: Joining and clearing
sections.body:
`table.concat(list, separator)` joins an array of strings or numbers into one string, putting the separator **between** items: no stray comma at the end. It's also much faster than joining in a loop with `..=` when there are many items.

`table.clear(list)` empties a table while keeping the same table, which matters when other code holds a reference to it. You'll see why references matter in lesson 4.

key_points: `for i, v in list do` loops over an array in order. `ipairs` does the same.
`table.find` returns an item's index, or `nil` if it's missing.
`table.sort` sorts in place, and a comparison function sets a custom order.
`table.concat` joins items with a separator between them.
mistakes: Expecting `table.sort` to return a sorted copy. It returns nothing and changes the list.
Using `table.concat` on a list containing booleans or tables, which errors.
lessons.try_it: Make a list of six delivery times in minutes. Sort them from slowest to fastest, print them joined with commas, and use `table.find` to check whether a time of 45 minutes is in the list.

quiz.question: What does `table.find({ "x", "y" }, "z")` return?
quiz.explain: It returns the index of a match, or nil when there isn't one.

quiz.question: `local s = table.sort(list)`. What is `s`?
choices: `nil`, because table.sort sorts the list in place and returns nothing
quiz.explain: table.sort changes the list itself, and returns nothing.

quiz.question: What does `table.concat({ "a", "b", "c" }, "-")` give?
quiz.explain: The separator goes between items only.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Tables with named keys, the two ways to read them, looping with pairs, and removing keys.

sections.heading: Keys and values
sections.body:
Arrays use numbers as keys. A **dictionary** uses any keys you like, most often strings, so a table can describe something with named fields. You write them inside curly brackets as `name = value` pairs.

Read a field with a dot, `order.customer`, or with square brackets and a string, `order["customer"]`. They're identical. The bracket form is needed when the key is in a variable, or isn't a valid name, like a key with a space in it.

example.caption: An order as a record
example.code:
local order = { customer = "Mrs Hill", pizzas = 2, paid = false }
print(order.customer, order["pizzas"])
order.paid = true
order.note = "Ring twice"
example.explain: Reads two fields, changes one, and adds a brand new field just by assigning to it.

sections.heading: Adding, changing and removing
sections.body:
Assigning to a key that doesn't exist yet adds it. Assigning to one that does changes it. And assigning `nil` **removes** the key, since tables can't hold `nil` values.

Reading a key that isn't there gives `nil`, just like with arrays. That's how you check whether a key exists: `if order.note then`. Be careful with fields that hold `false`, though, since `false` is falsy too. When `false` is a real value, compare with `~= nil`.

A neat consequence: dictionaries are perfect for things that may or may not have a value. A customer record can have a `note` field only when there's a note, and every reader simply checks whether it's there.

sections.heading: Looping over a dictionary
sections.body:
Generalised iteration works on dictionaries: `for key, value in order do` visits every key and value. So does `pairs(order)`, which you'll see in older code.

The order is **not** defined. Don't rely on keys coming out in the order you wrote them, or the same order each time. If order matters, keep the keys in an array and loop over that instead.

`#` doesn't count dictionary entries: it's for arrays, and gives 0 for a table with only named keys. To count entries, loop and add one each time.

sections.heading: Keys can be anything
sections.body:
Keys don't have to be strings. Any value except `nil` can be a key: numbers, booleans, even other tables and Roblox instances. Using a player as a key is how you'll store per-player data later on, like `coins[player] = 50`.

Two keys are the same only if they're equal with `==`. For tables and instances that means the **same** object, not one that looks the same. Two separate tables with identical contents are still two different keys.

key_points: Dictionaries map keys to values. `t.key` and `t["key"]` are the same.
Assign to add or change a key, and assign `nil` to remove it.
Looping over a dictionary visits every pair, in no particular order.
`#` doesn't count dictionary entries.
mistakes: Writing `t.key` when the key's name is stored in a variable. Use `t[variable]`.
Relying on the order of a dictionary loop.
Using `#` to count named keys and getting 0.
lessons.try_it: Make a dictionary of three customers' favourite pizzas. Print one by key, change one, remove one, then loop over the rest printing each pair. Count the remaining entries with a loop.

quiz.question: With `local key = "tip"`, which line reads the field named tip from `order`?
quiz.explain: order.key would look for a field literally named key. Brackets use the variable's value.

quiz.question: How do you remove the `note` field from a table?
quiz.explain: Assigning nil removes the key, since tables can't store nil.

quiz.question: What is `#{ a = 1, b = 2 }`?
quiz.explain: The length operator measures the array part, and this table has no numbered items.

lessons.title: Nested tables and references
lessons.summary: Tables inside tables, and the crucial fact that variables hold references to tables, not copies.

sections.heading: Tables inside tables
sections.body:
A table's values can be tables, which is how you model real data. A night's orders is an **array of records**: a list where each item is a dictionary with fields like customer and pizzas. You reach inside with chained lookups: the orders, then an index, then a field.

Loops and records work together naturally. Looping over the array gives you one record at a time, and inside the loop you read its fields by name.

example.caption: A list of records
example.code:
local orders = {
	{ customer = "Hill", pizzas = 2 },
	{ customer = "Vance", pizzas = 5 },
}
for _, order in orders do
	print(order.customer, order.pizzas)
end
example.explain: Each loop run gets one record, then reads its fields.

sections.heading: Variables hold references
sections.body:
This is the most important idea in the chapter. When you assign a table to a variable, the variable doesn't hold the table itself. It holds a **reference** to it, like an address. Assigning that variable to another variable copies the reference, not the table, so both names now point at the **same** table.

Change the table through one name and you see the change through the other. Numbers and strings don't behave like this, which is why it surprises people.

example.caption: Two names, one table
example.code:
local original = { pizzas = 2 }
local other = original
other.pizzas = 9
print(original.pizzas)
example.explain: Prints `9`. There was only ever one table.

sections.heading: Functions receive the same table
sections.body:
Passing a table to a function passes the reference too. So a function **can** change a table you give it, and the caller sees the change. That's useful, for example a `markPaid(order)` function that flips a field. But it's also a source of bugs when a function changes a table its caller didn't expect it to.

A good rule is to decide, for every function that takes a table, whether it changes it or not, and make that obvious from the name. `sortOrders` sounds like it sorts in place. `sortedCopy` sounds like it doesn't.

sections.heading: Copying and freezing
sections.body:
When you need an independent copy, use `table.clone(t)`. It makes a new table with the same keys and values. It's a **shallow** copy: if a value is itself a table, the copy holds a reference to that same inner table. Copying deeply nested data means cloning each level.

`table.freeze(t)` makes a table read-only, so any attempt to change it errors. Freezing a settings table protects it from accidental edits. Like clone, it's shallow: tables inside a frozen table can still change unless you freeze them too.

key_points: Arrays of records model real data: a list of dictionaries.
Variables hold references to tables. Assigning shares, it doesn't copy.
Functions receive the same table and can change it.
`table.clone` copies one level. `table.freeze` makes one level read-only.
mistakes: Thinking `local copy = original` makes a copy.
Sorting or changing a table passed into a function when the caller still needs the original.
Expecting `table.clone` to copy nested tables too.
lessons.try_it: Make an array of three order records. Write a function that doubles every order's pizzas, call it, and print the original array to see the change. Then make a clone first, change the clone, and check the original is untouched.

quiz.question: `local a = { 1 }` then `local b = a` then `b[1] = 5`. What is `a[1]`?
quiz.explain: a and b refer to the same table, so the change shows through both names.

quiz.question: After `local c = table.clone(a)`, does changing `c[1]` change `a`?
choices: No, c is a separate table
quiz.explain: clone makes a new table, so its top-level values are independent.

quiz.question: A table is frozen with `table.freeze`. What happens if you assign to one of its keys?
quiz.explain: Frozen tables are read-only, and writing to one is an error.

lessons.title: Sets, counts and lookup tables
lessons.summary: Using table keys for fast membership checks, counting things, and replacing if chains with data.

sections.heading: Sets
sections.body:
Sometimes you only care whether something is **in** a group, not where. Store each member as a **key** with the value `true`: that's a **set**. Checking membership is then a single lookup, `if banned[name] then`, which is instant however big the set gets.

Compare that with an array, where `table.find` has to check items one by one. For a handful of items it makes no difference, but for hundreds of checks per second, a set is the right tool. Removing a member is just assigning `nil`.

example.caption: Houses that don't answer
example.code:
local noAnswer = { [4] = true, [13] = true }
for house = 1, 5 do
	if noAnswer[house] then
		continue
	end
	print("Deliver to", house)
end
example.explain: Skips house 4, and checks membership with one lookup per house.

sections.heading: Counting things
sections.body:
To count how often each thing appears, use a dictionary as a tally: the thing is the key, and its count is the value. For each item, read the current count, treating a missing key as 0, add one, and store it back. The `or 0` default from chapter 3 makes that a one-liner.

This pattern answers questions like "how many orders did each customer place tonight" or "which pizza is most popular", and you'll use it constantly.

sections.heading: Lookup tables instead of if chains
sections.body:
An `if`/`elseif` chain that maps one value to another, like a topping to its price, can usually become a table. Store the mapping as data, `prices[topping]`, and the chain disappears.

The table version is shorter, easier to extend (adding a topping is one line), and can be changed without touching any logic. A missing key gives `nil`, so you handle unknown values in one place with a default.

example.caption: Prices as data
example.code:
local toppingPrice = { cheese = 0, mushroom = 1, ghost = 3 }
local function priceOf(topping)
	return toppingPrice[topping] or 2
end
print(priceOf("ghost"), priceOf("olive"))
example.explain: Prints `3 2`: olive isn't listed, so it gets the default price.

sections.heading: Choosing the right shape
sections.body:
Most data problems come down to picking a shape. An **array** when order matters or you want a list. A **dictionary** when you look things up by name. A **set** when you only ask "is it in there". An **array of records** for a list of things with fields.

Picking the right shape makes the code that uses it short and obvious. If your loops feel complicated, it's often a sign the data is in the wrong shape, and changing it fixes the code.

key_points: A set stores members as keys with the value `true`, for instant membership checks.
A tally dictionary counts things: read with `or 0`, add one, store back.
Lookup tables replace if chains that map values to values.
Choosing the right data shape keeps the code that uses it simple.
mistakes: Using `table.find` on a big array for frequent membership checks.
Forgetting the `or 0` default when counting, which errors on the first occurrence.
Writing long if chains for what is really a mapping.
lessons.try_it: Given a list of pizza names with repeats, build a tally of how many times each appears, then find the most popular one. Then turn an if chain that maps three sizes to prices into a lookup table with a default.

quiz.question: How do you add `"Vance"` to a set called `regulars`?
quiz.explain: In a set, members are keys with the value true.

quiz.question: What does `counts[name] = (counts[name] or 0) + 1` do the first time a name appears?
choices: Errors, because the key doesn't exist
quiz.explain: The missing key reads as nil, or turns it into 0, and adding one gives 1.

quiz.question: Why can a lookup table be better than an if chain for prices?
choices: It's the only way to store numbers
Adding a new item is one line of data, with no logic to change
If chains don't work with strings
quiz.explain: The mapping becomes data, so extending it doesn't touch the code.
